assigned.title: Stream candidate fields carry length bounds
assigned.acceptance: streamCandidateSchema bounds the length of its string fields, so a candidate cannot amplify a response. MEASURED, not hypothesised: a 1,000,000-character candidate id produced a 2,002,555-byte response during the PL-0702 review. The bound belongs in the contract rather than at the route, because every consumer of a candidate inherits it there and a per-route cap is one route away from being forgotten. Required: each bounded field's limit is justified against a real identifier rather than picked round -- state what the longest legitimate value looks like; a property test asserts no candidate accepted by the schema can exceed the response budget; and the change is checked against the fixture and Wikidata sources, because a bound that rejects a legitimate upstream id is an outage, not a fix. THE RISK THIS TASK CARRIES: streamCandidateSchema is the ranker's input and PL-0902 extends it; a bound set too low silently drops candidates and the reason trail must say so rather than showing an empty list. Out of scope: the request body bound (PL-0707).

unit.evidence: npx turbo run test --force, exit 0, 17 of 17, 0 cached, 2409 passed across the wave. Package: 8 files, 202 passed in contracts, 29 net-new tests (24 example, 5 property). RED with the tests written and the schema still z.string().min(1): 6 failed 50 passed, the three true reds being 'refuses the 1,000,000-character id that F11 measured', 'refuses an unbounded providerId on the same grounds' and 'does not echo the rejected value in the issue a route would return', each 'AssertionError: expected true to be false'. GREEN: 87 passed. THE NON-VACUITY GUARD CAUGHT THE IMPLEMENTER'S OWN TEST: the first green run was 2 failed, 'expected 325 to be greater than 744.5' -- the uniformly-mixed generator's largest ACCEPTED candidate was 325 bytes against a 1489-byte budget, so the budget property was passing without ever exercising the bound. A second deliberately-maximal branch was added. THE BOUNDS ARE DERIVED, NOT ROUND, and the derivation is in the code: providerId 64 because both producers already refuse above it (SOURCE_ID_PATTERN and FIXTURE_ID_PATTERN are each /^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]{0,63}$/i), so the contract cannot reject an id either adapter can mint; id 141 = 64+1+64+1+11 against Stremio's competing 64+1+8=73. Real ids measured: big-buck-bunny-progressive 26, wikidata-q83495-progressive 27. MAX_STREAM_CANDIDATE_JSON_BYTES 1489 decomposes exactly and an example test reconstructs the worst case so the literal cannot drift. NO SILENT DROP, which the acceptance names as the risk: all three enforcement points name the field and the limit, and zod's too_big does not echo the received value -- measured 180 bytes of response for a 1,000,000-character id, asserted as expect(body).not.toContain(payload). Consumers re-run green: media-engine 369 passed, provider-sdk mapping and health 67 passed. F11's MECHANISM CORRECTED IN THE CODE: the second copy is 'selected', not the reason trail, so an eligible candidate costs 2x and an ineligible one 1x via rejected[].candidateId; the measurement stands, its explanation did not.

assigned.title: Egress host classification folds the DNS root label
assigned.acceptance: packages/media-inspection/src/egress.ts classifies a fully qualified name the same as its dotless spelling, matching the fix PL-0702 made in packages/provider-sdk/src/stremio/url-policy.ts. THIS IS LOWER PRIORITY THAN IT SOUNDS AND THE REASON MUST NOT BE LOST: this path fails CLOSED -- an unrecognised spelling is refused rather than permitted -- so it is an inconsistency between two classifiers, not a bypass. It is filed anyway because two classifiers disagreeing about what a host is will eventually be reconciled by someone copying the wrong one. Required: the fix is the same narrowing (fold the root label before comparison, refuse an empty label rather than repairing it); a test asserts the two classifiers agree on a shared table of hostile spellings, so the next divergence fails a test rather than waiting for a review; and the fail-closed behaviour is preserved and asserted, because making this path agree with the other one must not make it permissive. Out of scope: merging the two classifiers into one, which is the resolve-and-pin question and belongs to PL-0710.

unit.evidence: npx turbo run test --force, exit 0, 17 of 17, 0 cached, 2409 passed across the wave. Package: 10 files, 226 passed, 191 pre-existing and 0 regressions. RED against unmodified egress.ts: 12 failed 23 passed, including 'expected url_host_not_on_egress_allowlist to be ok:public' and 'expected url_host_not_on_egress_allowlist to be url_loopback_not_permitted'. GREEN: 35 passed. A FINDING THE FIX PRODUCED, sharper than the one filed: before the change hostOnAllowlist('..', ['..']) returned TRUE, and so did hostOnAllowlist('cdn.example.test..', ['cdn.example.test..']) -- the old code treated a leading-dot entry as a suffix without validating it, so a string naming no host was matchable, and an entry repaired down to empty is the empty suffix, which matches every host there is. It never reached production behaviour because classifyHost refuses those with url_host_unparseable before the allowlist is consulted, so fail-closed held, but the function alone said yes. MUTATION-CHECKED: the tempting permissive fix, return host.replace(/\.+$/, '') -- fold until it stops instead of refusing -- makes 3 tests fail, so the fail-closed assertions are not vacuous. FAIL-CLOSED PRESERVED AND ASSERTED in both directions: empty allowlist still fetches nothing for every spelling in the table; the leading-dot rule still means strict subdomain; and the controls in front of and behind the allowlist still run, including url_host_private_literal for metadata.google.internal. EVEN WITH THAT HOST EXPLICITLY ALLOWLISTED. Folding admits exactly one thing that was refused before: another spelling of a name the operator already wrote down. The shared hostile-spelling table drives BOTH real implementations from one source, so the next divergence fails a test.
